series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals

rawEventDetails: Speaker Atsutse Kludze Details Event Description The sub-Terahertz (sub-THz) bands - frequencies above 100 GHz and up to 1 THz - are rapidly emerging as one of the accepted paradigms for future wireless networks. In principle, these frequencies can provide ultra-fast data transmission due to their large amount of available bandwidth. Nonetheless, several fundamental challenges stand in the way of their adoption. Instead of merely scaling the existing wireless system architecture, my thesis investigates how to leverage the physics of sub-THz signals to overcome these hurdles. One of the biggest obstacles is power consumption, since generating and amplifying signals above 100 GHz requires power-hungry circuitry. This issue is compounded by severe path loss, which demands highly directional links created by large antenna arrays. To address this, my thesis introduces LeakyScatter, a new passive architecture that enables wideband backscattering above 100 GHz. By exploiting leaky-wave antenna physics, LeakyScatter establishes retro-directive links without active components or power consumption. Power alone, however, does not determine scalability: sub-THz networks also demand devices that can be manufactured over large areas at low cost. To this end, I introduce a new class of broadband, electronically reconfigurable sub-THz metasurfaces whose active element is an organic electrochemical modulator. By electrochemically doping and de-doping large-area patterned organic films, these devices dynamically control the polarization, spectral response, and direction of sub-THz wavefronts at milliwatt-scale power, using fabrication processes compatible with large-area organic electronics. Next, given the emergence of high-frequency devices with electronically large aperture sizes, wireless users may fall into the near-field of an access point, where traditional far-field assumptions break down. I develop analytical and simulation frameworks to evaluate near-field beamforming performance and demonstrate how multiple coordinated arrays can overcome existing range and focusing limitations. Lastly, I explore how sub-THz signals can address pressing real-world challenges far beyond traditional wireless networking, enabling unprecedented sensing functionalities: non-coherent 3D localization from a single broadband transmission, and non-destructive fruit-quality monitoring that targets large-scale food waste where existing methods are invasive or economically impractical. Collectively, these efforts contribute foundational physical-layer architectures and device technologies for next-generation wireless networks. Adviser: Yasaman Ghasempour

series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Modern communication systems operate remarkably close to fundamental limits, but their design has historically relied on carefully engineered mathematical structure. rawEventDetails: Speaker Shibara Ashwin Hebbar Details Event Description Modern communication systems operate remarkably close to fundamental limits, but their design has historically relied on carefully engineered mathematical structure. Deep learning offers a complementary capability: learning representations and decision rules directly from data. Bringing this capability to communication, however, is difficult. In channel coding, for example, learning must generalize across an exponentially large message space that no practical training set can cover. This dissertation argues that classical structure and learned optimization play complementary roles in communication system design. It develops a framework of neural augmentation, in which learned components are embedded within classical systems. The classical design organizes computation, guides training, and constrains what learning may change, while learning is concentrated on the operation or representation that limits performance. We develop this principle at progressively deeper levels of the communication stack. TinyTurbo retains the Turbo decoding algorithm and learns a low-dimensional correction to the exchanged soft information, recovering much of the loss introduced by the max-log-MAP approximation. CRISP preserves the sequential structure of Polar and PAC decoding, but learns the conditional decision rules using a curriculum derived from nested subcodes, approaching the reliability of stronger classical decoders without list search or backtracking. DeepPolar goes further by learning the code itself together with a matched decoder. It replaces fixed binary Polar kernels with learned nonlinear transformations while retaining the recursive construction and successive decoding structure needed for scalability. The resulting codes improve reliability over classical Polar and Reed–Muller codes under successive-cancellation decoding. DeepOFDM extends neural augmentation from coding to modulation, replacing independent symbol-wise mappings with context-dependent neural modulation whose gains are largest under high mobility and sparse or absent pilots. Finally, we move iii beyond bit-level fidelity to task-aware source coding for vision-language receivers. Using the question as side information, FoCAL preserves task-relevant image detail and reduces rate by 28–57% at matched downstream performance while keeping the receiver frozen. A complementary codec adaptation transfers across multiple receivers without additional retraining. Across these systems, a consistent picture emerges: classical structure provides the architectural and training biases that make learning tractable, while learning improves the approximations and representations that classical design leaves suboptimal. Adviser: Pramod Viswanath

rawEventDetails: Speaker Manting Gui Details Event Description Organic solar cells and organic photodetectors combine mechanical flexibility, solution processability, and spectral tunability from the visible to the near infrared, yet their performance remains limited by large voltage losses and parasitic dark currents compared with inorganic counterparts. In donor–acceptor (D–A) heterojunction diodes, nonradiative recombination via charge transfer (CT) states broadened by energetic disorder is a key origin of voltage loss, but reliable approaches for quantifying CT state disorder are not yet well-recognized in the community. In parallel, intrinsic dark current generation is increasingly attributed to deep trap states, while its microscopic origin and the deviations from ideal diode behavior are still not fully clarified. This thesis investigates new nonradiative recombination and dark current generation pathways using a combination of steady state and spectroscopic techniques to characterize CT states, associated energy loss, and the thermal dependence of dark current and charge transport. Studies on a series of amorphous and crystalline organic diodes, and inorganic-organic hybrid diodes show that hole polarons play a central role in organic systems by introducing additional nonradiative energy loss channels and inducing extra dark current generation, detrimental for both photovoltaic and photodetector operation. A specific mechanism is identified in which NIR hole polarons act as antennas in D–A blends, facilitating thermal excitation of CT states and inherently driving dark current. The activation energy of the reverse saturation dark current is found to track the activation energy of hole polaron transport, highlighting polaron dynamics as a key control parameter. Overall, device behavior is rationalized as a coupled CT–polaron problem: under illumination, CT recombination governed by the energy gap law, together with CT-polaron spectral overlap, enhances voltage loss and fundamentally limits photocurrent; whereas in the dark, the spectral overlap of blackbody radiation with CT and polaron absorption sets an effective generation prefactor for the dark current. Finally, inorganic–organic hybrid diodes, exemplified by CuSCN/organic acceptor heterojunctions, exhibit substantially reduced dark currents relative to fully organic devices, indicating their potential for high detectivity near infrared photodetectors. Adviser: Barry Rand

rawEventDetails: Speaker Grace Cimaszewski Details Event Description HTTPS underpins secure communication on the Web, but its trust is bootstrapped through domain control validation (DV) : a challenge-response protocol through which Certificate Authorities (CAs) verify the requester' s control of a domain name. DV relies on unauthenticated protocols (including BGP, DNS, and HTTP), and is therefore vulnerable to network-level attacks that can enable fraudulent certificate issuance. This thesis hardens DV against network attacks through three deployable defenses spanning ecosystem-wide protection and opt-in cryptographic guarantees, and translates them into real-world standards and deployment. First, we quantify and strengthen multi-perspective issuance corroboration (MPIC). Using a custom full-graph DNS resolver, we present the first Internet-scale measurement of DV' s complete attack surface, covering 1. 1 M domains and over 31 billion DNS queries. Bringing DNS into scope drops single-perspective resilience from 86% to 38%; strategic placement of five diverse vantage points with a unanimous quorum policy restores it to 97%. These findings shaped CA/ Browser Forum Ballot SC-067v3, which standardized the core MPIC framework evaluated here and mandated it for server certificate issuance starting September 2025. MPIC has thus protected over 1. 5 billion certificates to date. Second, we present cryptographically-secure DV ("crypto-DV"), a framework providing cryptographic issuance guarantees for opt-in domains. Using DNSSEC trust roots, CAs boot-strap secure channels with domain owners and validate DV challenges with cryptographic integrity. A fail-closed CAA policy enforces this protection under partial deployment: non-implementing CAs must refuse issuance. Its deployment prerequisite, DNSSEC validation by CAs, was mandated by CA/ Browser Forum Ballot SC-085 v2 effective March 2026, and the design informed an IETF working-group draft. Third, we propose secure channel DNS, a scalable alternative to DNSSEC' s stalled per-zone adoption that secures resolver-nameserver communications via encrypted channels. Measuring ~449M domains from Certificate Transparency logs, we find that eight providers host authoritative DNS for 47.7% of measured domains, suggesting that deployment at a few operators could protect resolution for much of the Web. We analyze how SVCB records can support this abstraction and contribute an open-source implementation in Hickory DNS for deployment at Let' a Encrypt. Together, these results show a deployable path for authenticated DNS beyond DNSSEC. Adviser: Prateek Mittal

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Reshaping Light via Photon Up- and Down-Conversion Abstract : Due to its ability to transmit energy and information through space, light plays a central role in nearly all aspects of human society. However, light has a peculiar property as its energy content is transmitted by photons, discrete particles whose energy must be matched to their intended application. Materials that reshape light, by combining the energy of multiple low-energy photons or by using single high-energy photons to produce multiple lower energy ones, can enable new light-driven technologies and optoelectronics. In this presentation, I will highlight work by my group to design hybrid structures that interface organic molecules with inorganic nanocrystals and bulk solids for the purpose of reshaping light’s energy content. When properly assembled, these materials can facilitate photon upconversion, the creation of higher energy photons from pairs of low-energy ones, which has applications for bioimaging, light detection, and additive manufacturing. With some small design changes, energy can be made to flow in the opposite direction in these structures, achieving photon downconversion which can be used for solar energy harvesting, quantum information science, and catalysis. Much of the work that I will feature will focus on using ultrafast microscopy methods to track energy flow within these materials with femtosecond time-resolution and sub-micron spatial resolution. rawEventDetails: Speaker Michael Webb Affiliation Princeton University Details Event Description Polymers are essential to a wide range of technologies, yet designing them with targeted structural and functional properties remains a grand challenge. Moreover, the products and technology only exploit a fraction of the prospective design space availed by macromolecules. A major opportunity lies in applying machine learning to help navigate the vast combinatorial design space—spanning sequence, composition, architecture, morphology, processing, and more—to discover new formulations or replace existing ones with more sustainable alternatives. However, this complexity, combined with data scarcity and characterization challenges, limits the effectiveness of purely rational design and/or high-throughput screening. In this talk, I will describe some of our recent efforts to integrate molecular simulation, machine learning, and theory to map and navigate structure–function relationships in chemically and topologically diverse polymeric materials. I will describe strategies that we have employed across a range of applications to overcome data limitations in polymer science by developing physics-informed (or guided) models as well as other algorithmic innovations. Specific examples of our approach will be drawn from the characterization of single-chain nanoparticle morphologies, the design of enzyme-stabilizing copolymers, and the formulation of architecturally complex polymer additives that tune solution rheology. These examples will showcase utility, limitations, and opportunities for data-driven approaches in modern-day science and how coupling them with (or using them to develop) physical insight can accelerate innovation and deepen materials understanding.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Yakun Sophia Shao Affiliation University of California, Berkeley Details Event Description Abstract: Computing systems are becoming increasingly closed loop. A robot continuously senses, computes, and acts in the physical world; more broadly, emerging AI applications interact dynamically with users, tools, and environments. Yet the way we design these systems remains largely open loop: models, software, hardware architectures, and implementations are developed in separate stages, with slow and incomplete feedback across layers. As a result, improvements in isolated metrics such as kernel latency, energy, or hardware utilization do not necessarily translate into better end-to-end behavior. In this talk, I will argue that closing this gap requires rethinking both what we design and how we design it. The full computing stack should be treated as a connected, executable design space in which application goals, software, architecture, and implementation continuously inform one another. I will trace our efforts to close this loop: first by making cross-layer consequences observable in end-to-end applications, then by co-designing heterogeneous hardware and software around system-level requirements, and ultimately by using AI to navigate and accelerate the design process itself. I will conclude with a vision for using AI not simply to generate code or implementations, but to participate in system and architecture design itself. By making design choices, constraints, and feedback explicit and machine-operable, we can move toward a closed-loop methodology that connects application goals to deployable systems, from mission to silicon. Bio: Professor Yakun Sophia Shao is The Class of 1951 Chair Associate Professor at the Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences department of University of California, Berkeley. Her research interests are in the area of computer architecture, with a special focus on specialized accelerator, heterogeneous architecture, and agile VLSI design methodology. Previously, she was a Senior Research Scientist at NVIDIA Research and received her Ph.D. degree in 2016 from Harvard University. She is a recipient of the 2025 Outstanding Teaching Award in EE, the 2024 Anita Borg Early Career Award, a Sloan Research Fellowship, an NSF CAREER Award, the 2022 IEEE TCCA Young Computer Architect Award, a Google Faculty Rising Stars Award in Systems Research, a Google Research Scholar Award, a Facebook Research Award, an Okawa Foundation Research Grant, and the inaugural Dr. Sudhakar Yalamanchili Award. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Traditional hard clustering methods fail to capture the complex, overlapping risk linkages present in modern markets. While recent work (Ding et al., 2024) identifies broad block structures in stock co-jumps, we demonstrate that this framework can be significantly enhanced by incorporating mixed membership. Specifically, we propose a Degree Corrected Mixed Membership network model with Dependent Multivariate Poisson edges that allows stocks to belong to multiple latent risk communities simultaneously and a corresponding estimation algorithm. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Large-scale causal mediation, replication, and pleiotropy analyses may appear to be unrelated problems. However, they all involve testing a large number of composite null hypotheses, a statistically challenging task arising in many scientific settings, especially in genomic and biobank studies. A composite null is defined as the union of K individual null hypotheses, and is rejected only when all individual hypotheses are false. We will first show that classical tests such as Wald and likelihood ratios fail to follow chi-square tests and are often overly conservative, leading to substantial power loss. We propose several approaches to address this problem. We show that the divide-aggregate composite-null test (DACT) by leveraging a large number of tests and Efron’s empirical null framework works well when signals are weak and sparse, but can exhibit error rate inflation in the presence of dense and strong signals. To overcome this limitation, we propose a tail likelihood ratio (TLR) test that is robust and powerful across diverse settings, encompassing weak to strong signal strengths, sparse to dense signal proportions, symmetric and unsymmetric signal distributions, and correlations among the large number of tests. We show that local FDR for a large number of composite nulls can be expressed as a function of a likelihood ratio, which is approximated in the tail region to construct the TLR statistic. We derive the null distribution of the TLR statistic by leveraging information from the large number of tests, and account for correlation among tests using a principal component-based approximation. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed method maintains accurate error rate control in multiple comparisons and exhibits superior power gains compared to existing methods. Applications to multiple examples further illustrate the performance and utility of the proposed framework.

Rich Sutton's 'bitter lesson' states that "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective" in AI. The corollaries are bittersweet in chemistry and materials. The tremendous success of universal ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs) as surrogate for quantum-mechanical energies and forces is unarguable. Trained on 100-million-count datasets, they reflect scaling laws similar to the ones in language or vision models, generalizing to new scientific questions and enabling simulations that were intractable a few years ago. Generative models, trained mostly on the same synthetic data, are currently being used to propose novel materials at machine speed. The discussion around the power of inductive bias (energy conservation, equivariance) and whether it is better reflected in model architecture or in training strategy is very much ongoing. The physical sciences may well be the last holdout for domain knowledge and inductive bias, or maybe they will ultimately follow the same trends as other domains. But MLIPs are surrogates for physics-based simulators, and arguably, materials only truly matter if they are made in the lab and then scaled up industrially and commercially. This is the truly bitter scaling lesson in materials. The promise of AI for chemistry and materials needs to be realized through very traditional, expensive and slow channels. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Integration of statistics and generative AI plays a pivotal role for accelerating trustworthy cross-domain scientific discovery. Recent advances in generative models have dramatically increased the availability and use of synthetic data across scientific domains. While these developments create exciting opportunities for empowering data analysis, they also raise fundamental statistical challenges regarding how synthetic data can be used in a valid, reliable, and principled manner. In this talk, we first discuss the current landscape of high-fidelity high-dimensional synthetic data generation using generative AI models such as transformer, diffusion, and flow matching based models. More importantly, we present a principled framework for incorporating synthetic data in downstream statistical analysis that ensures valid statistical inference even when generative AI models are misspecified. We show that the proposed synthetic data assisted and augmented methods for continuous and discreate outcomes that integrate observed and synthetic data are robust to misspecified black-box generative models and can improve statistical inferential power when the generative AI models are informative. We demonstrate the utility of these synthetic data assisted methods to the analysis of the UK biobank data, by performing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of proteomic data and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analyses of brain imaging phenotypes, and binary mental health survey data both characterized by substantial missingness (about 70-90%). title: Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract Modern LLMs scale at test-time, e.g. via repeated sampling, where inference cost grows with model size and the number of samples. This creates a trade-off that pretraining scaling laws, such as Chinchilla, do not address. In this talk, we present Train-to-Test (T^2) scaling laws that jointly optimize model size, training tokens, and number of inference samples under fixed end-to-end budgets. T^2 modernizes pretraining scaling laws with pass@k modeling used for test-time scaling, then jointly optimizes pretraining and test-time decisions. Forecasts from T^2 are robust over distinct modeling approaches: measuring joint scaling effect on the task loss and modeling impact on task accuracy. Across eight downstream tasks, we find that when accounting for inference cost, optimal pretraining decisions shift radically into the overtraining regime, well-outside of the range of standard pretraining scaling suites. We validate our results by pretraining heavily overtrained models in the optimal region that T^2 scaling forecasts, confirming their substantially stronger performance compared to pretraining scaling alone. Finally, as frontier LLMs are post-trained, we show that our findings survive the post-training stage, making T^2 scaling meaningful in modern deployments. title: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
content: Video
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Today's reasoning models use thinking tokens to attain stronger performance on benchmarks than their instruction-tuned counterparts. It is also generally believed that this more "deliberative" mode should improve alignment and safety, by providing the model a safe space to consider whether its planned answer to a request violates its safety principles. We present evidence that this intuition is not always correct. Across frontier open-weight reasoning models spanning GPT-OSS, Qwen, Olmo, and Phi families, we find that the eventual refusal/compliance outcome is already strongly predictable via a trained head on the first token's hidden representation (0.84-0.95 AUROC and ∼88% balanced accuracy for predicting refusal/compliance) before any visible thinking. The thinking process turns out to be more akin to prefix completion than to deliberative revision, with the final outcome rarely changing after the first ∼20% of thinking, despite giving the appearance of deliberation at the text level (∼74% of text-level deliberations occur when the response distribution is already locked to one refusal/compliance side). We also find that existing inference-time and training-based safety interventions, despite being motivated by the goal of inducing deliberation, largely shift model behavior toward over-refusal while suppressing already-scarce deliberation signals. Our results suggest that safety behavior in current reasoning models is much less deliberative than commonly assumed, and highlight the need for methods that induce real safety deliberation. Bio : Narutatsu Ri is a second-year Ph.D. student advised by Professor Sanjeev Arora. His research focuses on the safety and alignment of large foundation models, with particular interests in measuring and mitigating misalignment, scalable oversight, and the safety implications of self-improving AI systems. content: Superconducting qubits are artificial atoms whose properties are shaped through the engineering of nonlinear electrical circuits. rawEventDetails: Speaker Parth Jatakia Details Event Description Superconducting qubits are artificial atoms whose properties are shaped through the engineering of nonlinear electrical circuits. Quantum information is encoded by selecting two levels of this multilevel system to form the computational subspace. Thus, standard operations can inadvertently populate states outside this subspace, producing leakage errors. In transmons, for example, increasing the resonator drive during readout can activate multiphoton resonances that induce measurement-induced state transitions (MISTs), transferring population to high-lying states and severely reducing measurement fidelity. MISTs therefore constrain attempts to make dispersive readout simultaneously faster and more accurately. Fluxonium pushes this engineering further, suppressing several sources of decoherence within the computational subspace. This produces an unusually rich, strongly anharmonic spectrum in which higher levels can couple more strongly to microwave fields, without the simple nearest-neighbour selection structure of transmons. The first part of this dissertation examines how MISTs arise in fluxonium and what sets their magnitude. Using flux-pulse-assisted measurements, we uncover population transfer that multiphoton resonances alone cannot explain. To explain them, we perform time-dependent open-quantum-system simulations incorporating driven multilevel dynamics and dissipation. The simulations reveal a new decay-assisted pathway for MISTs: the readout drive populates hybridized states involving higher fluxonium levels, while decay redirects population into the excited qubit manifold. We find that the combined action of drive and decay produces an optical-pumping-like transfer that builds up over the measurement pulse. Multiphoton resonances therefore provide pathways for MISTs, while their magnitude depends continuously on the drive protocol and the environment. The second part of this work examines this environment and the processes through which it exchanges energy with the qubit. Existing fluxonium loss models are phenomenological and cannot by themselves pinpoint the microscopic process or material source of dissipation. We therefore measure excitation and relaxation separately, resolving the environment’s ability to supply and absorb energy. Their imbalance defines a transition-specific effective temperature, while flux tunability turns the rates into a spectral probe of the environment. Across frequency and devices, the directed rates reveal substantial variation, underscoring the complexity of the environment governing qubit dissipation. Adviser: Andrew Houck

Design and optimization of such materials require understanding how subtle variations in molecular composition and organization change this balance. However, this relationship is often difficult to predict as macroscopic properties originate from many interactions occurring at length and time scales far smaller than those directly observed. Molecular simulations provide a means to bridge this gap by relating molecular-level behavior to material response. This dissertation combines physics-based molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and data-driven machine learning techniques to investigate how molecular chemistry governs physical properties across diverse organic condensed-phase systems, particularly molecular liquids and polymeric materials. In the case of molecular liquids, the central challenge is determining how strongly nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) influence thermophysical properties across chemical space. For polymeric materials, the challenge lies in resolving how functional group chemistry, mixture composition, and comonomer sequence underlie distinct physical phenomena in structurally complex systems. The studies presented here address distinct challenges in relating molecular chemistry to macroscopic properties in complex condensed-phase systems. Together, these insights provide molecular-level principles for understanding physical phenomena and help guide the rational design of high-performance materials.

Developed mainly by Brazilian scientists, this model has been used for scientific research, policymaking, and forest conservation. It also provided the technical foundation for South America’s first REDD+ forest carbon project and the world’s first REDD+ carbon accounting methodology. However, in the process of international validation of this REDD+ carbon accounting methodology, the validation agencies, all from Europe and North America, imposed technical requirements, such as smaller Minimum Mapping Units and higher satellite-imaging resolution, that were disconnected from the geographical scales and technological capacities of tropical rainforest countries. Zhang analyzes how AI development and use are constrained by knowledge hegemony and North-South inequality in the postcolonial world. Finally, moving beyond political-economic or ethical debates, Zhang suggests an epistemologically reflexive approach of decolonizing or indigenizing science for better human knowledge production today. Nissenbaum’s research takes an ethical perspective on policy, law, science, and engineering related to information technology, computing, digital media, and data science. Topics have included privacy, trust, accountability, security, and values in technology design. Her books include “Obfuscation: A User’s Guide for Privacy and Protest” with Finn Brunton and “Privacy in Context: Technology, Policy, and the Integrity of Social Life.” Grants from the NSF , AFOSR , and the U.S. DHHS-ONC have supported her work. She was a recipient of the 2014 Barwise Prize of the American Philosophical Association and an honorary doctorate from Leuphana University, Germany. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: We study a system of interacting diffusions with heterogeneous pairwise interactions, so the particle system is non-exchangeable. In the first part of the talk, we develop a quantitative, non-asymptotic approach to mean field approximation by comparing the law of any subcollection of particles with a suitably chosen product measure and proving sharp relative entropy bounds. The proof uses a BBGKY hierarchy adapted to the non-exchangeable setting and an unexpected connection with first-passage percolation. In the second part, we establish a universal central limit theorem for the global fluctuation field around the McKean-Vlasov limit. Under suitable structural and denseness conditions on the interaction matrix, the fluctuations converge to the same Gaussian SPDE as in the classical exchangeable mean field case. For $m_n$-regular graphs, this holds when $m_n/\sqrt n\to\infty$, and a spatial interaction model shows that the $n^{-1/2}$ denseness threshold is sharp. The proof builds on the sharp propagation of chaos estimates developed in the first part, together with functional inequalities and an analysis in negative Sobolev spaces. Based on joint work with Daniel Lacker and Fuzhong Zhou, and on joint work with Mykhaylo Shkolnikov. Short Bio : Lane Chun Yeung is a postdoctoral research associate at Carnegie Mellon University, mentored by Mykhaylo Shkolnikov. He received his Ph.D. in Operations Research from Columbia University, where he was advised by Daniel Lacker and Ioannis Karatzas. His research interests include interacting particle systems, mean field models, mathematical finance, and stochastic control and games. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Min-norm interpolators naturally arise as implicitly regularized limits of modern neural networks and other widely used algorithms. While their out-of-distribution risk has recently been analyzed in settings where test samples are unavailable during training, many practical applications allow partial access to target data. The behavior of min-norm interpolation in such settings remains poorly understood. In this talk, I will present a sharp characterization of the risk of min-norm interpolators under both covariate and model shifts. Our results yield several important insights. For instance, in the presence of model shift, incorporating additional data can actually harm prediction performance when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. Conversely, for higher signal-to-noise ratios, transfer learning is beneficial, provided the shift-to-signal ratio remains below a precise threshold, which I will define. To reach these conclusions, we develop novel anisotropic local laws, representing new advances in random matrix theory for heterogeneous data problems. I will also discuss applications of our results to the challenge of combining real data with synthetic data generated by AI models. This talk is based on joint works with Anvit Garg, Kenny Gu, Yanke Song, Debarghya Mukherjee, and Pragya Sur. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Organic Solvent Reverse Osmosis Membranes for Complex Mixture Separations Abstract : In this talk, the potential for membrane materials to reduce energy and carbon requirements for the separation of hydrocarbon feedstocks and products will be discussed. We developed a series of polymer materials that feature rigid polymer backbones with engineered mobility and functionality. We imbue the polymers with resistance to dilation induced by hydrocarbon immersion without the loss of solution-based membrane fabrication techniques. rawEventDetails: Speaker Christopher Burcham Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Crystal engineering has been used within the pharmaceutical industry for multiple decades, primarily applied to batch processes. Crystal engineering is employed for the control of crystal attributes such as crystal form, particle size, particle morphology as well as impurity rejection. While applied across intermediate steps, crystal engineering is often utilized for the isolation of the active pharmaceutical ingredient, as these particle attributes can directly impact the bioavailability of the drug when used in solid oral dosage forms. Concurrent with the increased utilization of particle engineering techniques, the pharmaceutical industry has also rediscovered continuous processing and as a natural result there has been an increased interest in continuous crystallization and isolation of pharmaceutical intermediates and APIs. Continuous crystallization presents unique challenges to the control of physical properties of active pharmaceutical ingredients by direct crystallization when compared to batch crystallization processes. These limitations can be overcome to some extent by the implementation of in-situ milling and other process intensification technologies. Development of these processes has historically been experiential through trial-and-error experimentation – which leads to long development cycles, and the need for significant quantities of materials to fund the development studies. Application and utilization of population balance models (PBM) significantly decrease both the development cycle time and the material needs – a case study demonstrating the efficiency gains of using PBMs will be presented. While the utilization of PBMs greatly decreases the development timeframe, the overall process development cycle is quite linear, such that the development of the process cannot begin until many other activities are completed, all of which rely on the selection of the crystal form that will be carried forward – which until recently has been done through extensive crystal screening studies. Innovations in ab-initio crystal structure predictions (CSP) offer the promise of transforming polymorph screening and selection by predicting all possible polymorphs of a given organic molecule along with the associated free energies of each predicted form. These advances in the ability to predict crystal form as well as crystal growth have progressed to such a point where one can ask – can the linear process development workflow be replaced through in-silico simulations? (Burcham et al, 2024). An in-silico workflow for the digital design of crystallization processes starting from the chemical structure of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) through to process development will be presented. The opportunities, current limitations and prospects for future innovation of this approach will be discussed. 1. Burcham, C. L., et al. (2024). rawEventDetails: Speaker Yaniv Romano Affiliation Technion- Israel Institute of Technology Details Event Description ECE KORHAMMER SEMINAR SERIES Abstract AI models are powerful, yet their use in practice raises two fundamental challenges. The first is trust: how can we make reliable inferences from black-box models when we only have a few reference examples to rely on? The second is steerability: how can we guide AI generation when we can recognize the outputs we prefer but cannot precisely quantify our preferences? In this talk, I will show how statistics and AI can empower one another to tackle both challenges. The first part focuses on reliable inference under limited data. I'll introduce General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI), a framework that safely enhances the sample efficiency of any statistical inference procedure—such as conformal prediction and hypothesis testing—by adaptively leveraging synthetic data. GESPI provides distribution-free error control regardless of synthetic-data quality while improving utility when those data are informative. I'll demonstrate its applicability across domains ranging from predictive uncertainty quantification to principled win-rate evaluation of large reasoning models. I'll also discuss how these ideas can support large-scale scientific discovery with false discovery rate control. In the second part, I'll introduce Preference-based Metropolis-Hastings (Pref-MH): a model-steering framework that leverages pairwise votes from an LLM judge to generate data satisfying complex properties of interest. Pref-MH exploits a novel connection between MH and the Bradley-Terry preference model. This connection enables rigorous steering of a base AI generator toward a target distribution that favors outputs preferred by the judge, without ever needing to estimate the judge's latent reward. Finally, I'll demonstrate Pref-MH in molecular design and show how the resulting synthetic data improve downstream inference when incorporated into GESPI. Bio Yaniv Romano is an associate professor in the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Computer Science at the Technion. He is also affiliated with NVIDIA as a visiting professor. Previously, he was a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Statistics at Stanford University. Yaniv holds a PhD, an MSc, and a BSc in electrical engineering, all from the Technion. His super-resolution technology, invented with Peyman Milanfar, has been integrated into Google’s flagship products, including Pixel phones. His uncertainty quantification method, developed with Emmanuel Candès, was used by The Washington Post to estimate outstanding votes during the U.S. presidential election. Yaniv has received several honors and awards, including an ERC Starting Grant, the SIAG/IS Early Career Prize, the Sheila Samson Prime Minister’s Prize (Researcher Recruitment Prize), the IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, the Alon Scholarship, the Krill Prize for Excellence in Scientific Research, and the Henry Taub Prize for Academic Excellence. Abstract: Molecular polaritons emerge when ensembles of molecules strongly couple to confined electromagnetic modes, enabling repeated energy exchange between light and matter. Such interactions are expected to activate nonlinear optical processes, yet many experimental observations remain accurately described by classical optics. We address this paradox from a spectroscopic perspective. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Electrifying energy-intensive industries is a key component of reducing fossil fuel consumption and meeting decarbonization goals, but these end uses have been slower to transition than other sectors of the economy because of the diversity of industrial processes, the heat and temperature requirements involved, and the capital-intensive nature of existing infrastructure. Our object of interest is not estimating the average treatment effect, but recovering the full treated distribution in the target site using transfer knowledge from the source site, while allowing cross-site heterogeneity in measurement systems, observed features, outcome reporting, population composition, and latent contextual factors. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. Suspensions are found in many forms and settings, and the compositions and properties can vary widely. However, certain issues prevail: one is the influence of the liquid through hydrodynamic interactions, and a second is the importance of the solid fraction and interparticle forces in controlling the flow properties, which we usually call the rheology of the material. Suspensions include colloidal dispersions of nanoparticles as well as cases involving somewhat larger particles such as cement, ceramics, and mud. The last three are all examples of dense suspensions, with solid fraction approaching the limit of flowability known as jamming. Because the rheology most often depends on the magnitude of the applied forces (e.g. pressure gradient in a pipe flow), suspensions are complex fluids – or they may be unyielded soft solids that can be caused to flow by enough force, as seen in the examples of cement mortars or muds. Here, we will present results based on simulations of suspensions approaching jamming to illustrate the unique features of these materials. These include discontinuous shear thickening (DST) as well as shear-induced jamming. The role of interparticle forces, including conservative and frictional contact forces, and the imposed stress in this process will be briefly reviewed, followed by our current examination of structures that are found to be related to the abrupt flow transitions. On approach to jamming, these structures develop as a result of the progressive reduction of the particle degrees of freedom in their motion as networks of contacts are formed. These networks rapidly break and reform during flow, but give rise to strongly correlated near-rigid motions of identifiable domains or “transient clusters.” The resulting fluctuations in motion become dominant as jamming is approached. In the DST regime, the contact number is found to fluctuate very strongly, but can result in highly connected but once again transient structures; system-spanning, or percolating, structures of frictionally-contacting particles are found to have important influence on the observed rheology.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Reimagining Thermochemical Catalysis: Promoting Reactions with Electric Fields Abstract : Catalysis has long relied on conventional handles such as temperature, pressure, and concentration to accelerate chemical reactions. Across biology and electrochemistry, electric fields provide an additional parameter to control rates. Enzymes exploit strong, oriented fields within their active sites to stabilize intermediates and accelerate turnover, while in electrochemistry, interfacial polarization dictates electron and proton transfer rates. In heterogeneous thermochemical catalysis, however, little is known about these effects, yet they may offer new opportunities to control reactivity. In this talk, I will describe our group’s efforts to harness electric fields to promote thermochemical reactions. For many electrochemical half-reactions, varying the applied potential accelerates rates by driving rate-controlling proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps. We hypothesized that if an elementary PCET step were embedded within a thermochemical reaction, its strong potential dependence could be leveraged to enhance the overall rate. Because interfacial PCET involves proton exchange across the electric double layer, we anticipated that Brønsted acid catalysis, governed by proton transfer, would be particularly susceptible to polarization. First, I will show how spontaneous interfacial fields at conductive particles dispersed in liquid media can measurably modulate turnover rates. Next, I will discuss how applied potentials produce reversible, exponential rate promotion in acid-catalyzed alcohol dehydration, accelerating rates by up to five orders of magnitude while the overall catalytic cycle remains non-Faradaic. Our kinetic analyses reveal that this acceleration arises from a field-driven increase in the population of reactive intermediates prior to the rate-determining step, providing a mechanistic basis for log-linear rate scaling with potential. I will then examine how electrolyte concentration and solvent properties set the interfacial potential profile and the fraction of the potential drop sampled by proton transfer, which separates electrostatic promotion from conventional solvent effects. In highly polar solvents, even trace ionic species can place nominally electrolyte-free reactions in a strongly suppressed regime through the catalyst's native open-circuit potential. Finally, I will highlight our development of polarized slurry reactors, which extend these principles from 2D electrodes to 3D catalyst slurries and enable rate enhancements under conditions more suitable for scale-up. These results establish interfacial electric fields and catalyst potential as design variables for controlling thermochemical reactivity and developing scalable catalytic processes. His research group designs heterogeneous catalysts and functional materials to tackle sustainability challenges in energy and chemicals. His group pioneered the use of electric fields to promote thermochemical reactions, developed catalytic routes to convert lignin into drop-in sustainable aviation fuel components, established the analytical and reactor engineering foundations for the chemical recycling of polyolefins, and created data-driven tools to predict zeolite synthesis. rawEventDetails: Speaker Chinedum Osuji Affiliation University of Pennsylvania Details Event Description Ion transport under nanoscale confinement and in the presence of charge is poorly understood from a fundamental perspective. Under the conditions of dielectric saturation that arise in nanoscale pores, the classical ideas that guide our understanding of electrostatic interactions break down, and new principles that account for the role of pore geometry and chemistry on water structure and ion interactions are needed. At the same time, our ability to develop such principles is hindered by the challenge of generating relevant well-defined geometries that enable experimental studies over statistically meaningful volumes such that experimental data can be more confidently considered alongside data from computational efforts. Beyond the fundamental implications, new understanding is needed to drive the rational design of materials for ion separations in critical minerals production and resource recovery, among other examples, where the need to distinguish between ions of the same valency and charge imposes a severe challenge. Here, we examine transport of ions in polymer membranes with well-defined sub-1 nm pores. The membranes are charged, modestly hydrated nanoporous polymers produced by crosslinking self-assembled lyotropic mesophases with direct hexagonal and gyroid nanostructures. This work addresses the roles of hydration, pore geometry and ion identity on transport using a combination of electrochemical and NMR measurements, and molecular simulation. Our results highlight the roles of hydration, solubility, pore size, and ion-pore wall interactions in dictating transport in the pores. They provide new insight regarding transport under nanoscale confinement in the presence of charge and that we suggest could be relevant for the development of materials for challenging ion separations.

rawEventDetails: Speaker Akshay Gadre Affiliation University of Washington Details Event Description Abstract: Almost every wireless device transmits over the air to communicate, and an increasing fraction of these devices can also use their signals to sense the physical world. As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is moving from research into standards, these radios periodically sense the world from the response of the environment on their transmitted signal. At the same time, WiFi, cellular, and automotive platforms are expanding into millimeter-wave spectrum, where wide bandwidths and compact antenna arrays provide fine spatial and temporal resolution, Together, these trends create the foundation for an Internet of Radar Things (IoRT) : a dense population of access points, base stations, vehicles, robots, and mobile devices whose radios can sense while they communicate. Unfortunately, a network of these sensing-capable radios operates largely as n isolated monostatic sensors: each independently occupies spectrum, illuminates an overlapping environment, and retains only the echoes at its own small aperture. These discarded paths contain complementary viewpoints that could extend coverage through occlusions, distinguish physical objects from multipath ghosts, and synthesize apertures far larger than any individual device. This talk presents a unique vision to coordinate these distributed radars coherently to turn this world of radios into one mega-radar. In this talk, we will first present the unique capabilities such a coherent future could enable and how we achieve coherence on commodity off-the-shelf radars to demonstrate these solutions. We specifically show how distributed radars can eliminate ghost artifacts and improve sensing capability, how we can extract material characteristics of objects using this large aperture and how we can use coherence-in-motion to develop free-flowing hand-held imaging solutions for mmWave radars. We further demonstrate how these improvements can directly translate to WiFi and cellular radios. Finally, we end the talk by describing open challenges that still need to be addressed to unleash the true potential of the Internet of Radar Things. Bio: Akshay Gadre is an Assistant Professor at Electrical and Computer Engineering department at the University of Washington. He leads the Networking and Emerging Wireless Technologies (NEWT) Lab at the University of Washington where they explore the upcoming application domains such as satellite IoT, mmWave radars and underwater devices, to apply wireless expertise for improving communication and sensing capability of these devices while preserving the security and privacy of sensor data. Further, the lab explores novel interaction mechanisms for future smart devices such as smart gloves and XR systems using novel force sensing and gaze modalities. His previous research at Carnegie Mellon University operated at the intersection of wireless, mobile and cyber-physical systems with special focus on empowering the low-power Internet-of-Things devices deployed on earth and space. NEWT Lab is also translating these technologies to industry partners including General Motors and IDD Aerospace. His work is published in premier wireless and mobile systems venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, Transactions on Sensor Networks and NSDI. Their lab's work has won two best paper awards, four best demo awards, two best-demo runner up awards at these venues. Both Akshay and his students have received the best PhD Forum presentation award at the CPS-IoT Week. Their work has been recognized with the T-Mobile T-Challenge 2024 Most Engaging Presentation Award for their vision of radio digital twins for consumer applications as well as the AFRL SDR University Challenge Best Demo award for developing a cheap SDR platform for exploring satellite networking. He has been also recognized with the ACM SIGBED-SIGSOFT Frank Anger Memorial Award 2021 for his cross-disciplinary work on IoT networking, cyber-security and software engineering. He was also recognized as a Distinguished TPC Member for his services to ACM SenSys 2026. He received his Bachelor of Technology (Honors) and Master of Technology degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from IIT Madras as well as a Ph.D in Electrical and Computer Engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Critical Materials Processing via Closed-Loop Redox-Mediated Leaching Abstract: Electrification can transform the way chemical reagents are produced, regenerated, and integrated into industrial processes. In hydrometallurgy, electrochemical regeneration of redox carriers enables closed-loop redox-mediated leaching (CL-RML), changing the relationship between reagent selection, process performance, and sustainability. Rather than treating oxidants or reductants as consumable reagents, CL-RML allows redox carriers to be selected primarily for their extraction performance and selectivity. This seminar will discuss a framework of closed-loop redox chemistry and discuss how it expands the design space for critical-materials extraction. Recent studies of nickel and copper extraction from sulfide minerals will be presented to illustrate how electrochemically regenerated redox carriers enable new opportunities to control mineral transformations, improve selectivity, and rethink process architecture. These examples demonstrate how regeneration influences not only leaching chemistry, but also upstream and downstream processes. By leveraging scalable industrial electrochemical technologies, closed-loop redox chemistry offers a pathway toward more modular, flexible extraction processes capable of treating increasingly complex mineral resources. Together, these concepts suggest that the greatest opportunity of CL-RML may be to expand the chemical and process design space available for future critical-minerals supply chains while simultaneously improving sustainability. rawEventDetails: Speaker Hong Yang Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Meeting the growing demand for energy requires the development of innovative energy conversion and storage processes beyond conventional thermal technologies and electrocatalysis plays a central role in this transition. While electrocatalysis shares a number of common design principles with thermal catalysis, they also differ greatly. Besides reactivity and selectivity, durability and stability under electrochemical reaction conditions are required for an electrocatalyst. In addition, electrochemical processes often occur at liquid-solid interface under potential, posting new challenges in design. In this presentation, I will discuss our research effort, aiming at uncovering structural design for electrocatalysts. Specifically, I will present the studies on structural and interfacial control of metal oxide and alloy electrocatalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER) which occurs in a range of chemical processes, such as hydrogen production from water splitting. Our finding suggests defect engineering is often central in the design of high-performance electrocatalysts for site and crystalline phase tunable complex oxides (i.e., rutile, pyrochlore, and perovskite) and for strained alloys. Flexibility in lattice of complex oxides (A x B y O z ) and tunability of surface strain of alloys often provide the controls of surface and lattice structures that affect the electrocatalytic reaction pathways and performance. Notably, unlike thermal catalysts, proper design of structural defects could simultaneously enhance both activity and stability of electrocatalysts. Valence band analysis, in situ Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, molecular probe and isotope kinetic studies, together with electrochemical characterizations, have been used to identify reactive intermediates and to understand reaction mechanisms.

speaker: Shira Zilberstein

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a promising solution to healthcare challenges, yet its clinical benefits still remain uncertain and its risks persistent. Drawing on extensive fieldwork with researchers developing machine-learning applications for healthcare, this talk demonstrates how practitioners sustain AI’s legitimacy by framing their work as serving the common good. It is argued that “moralization”—the work of aligning technological projects with values such as equity, care, and wellbeing—generates consensus and momentum for technological solutions to social problems amid uncertainty. At the same time, the moralization of machine learning risks obscuring technical limitations, diffusing accountability, and diverting attention from alternative approaches. Using healthcare AI to illuminate broader transformations in scientific authority as knowledge production becomes increasingly applied, interdisciplinary, and problem-oriented, it is shown how technical authority is established not through claims of neutrality or detachment, but by building relationships across institutional and professional boundaries. Bio: Shira Zilberstein is a sociologist whose research investigates the moral and organizational foundations of knowledge production, with particular attention to how science and technology are used to define and address social problems. Her current work focuses on the development and governance of AI models for healthcare. Using qualitative methods, she studies how researchers and practitioners justify and seek to ensure the social value of their work. She is especially interested in how research communities navigate uncertainty and sustain commitments to technological innovation even in the face of contested outcomes and limitations. Shira holds a Ph.D. in sociology from Harvard University, where she was a Science and Technology Studies Fellow and a BA in sociology and history from Northwestern University. Her research has been supported by the National Science Foundation, the American Sociological Association, the Russell Sage Foundation, and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, among others. She has collaborated with researchers at MIT, Duke, and Yale on projects related to the development and governance of healthcare AI. AI-based tools are projected to transform every stage of the research pipeline, from literature review and hypothesis generation, to the production of synthetic data and data analysis. Increasingly, with the rise of generative AI, AI tools are also put forward as means of arbitration over the scientific research process itself. Such proposals are being put into practice almost as quickly as they can be described, with little oversight or input from relevant expert communities. The workshop seeks to fill this gap by convening scholars with relevant expertise to weigh in on the prospects of AI in science evaluation and its potential ramifications for the future of science. We believe that this timely conversation must include spokespeople from artificial intelligence—both academic and industry, executives and editors at major journals and publishing houses, working scientists, metascientists, and scholars coming from history, philosophy, and sociology of science. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Thermal conductivity is a basic and familiar property of materials: silver spoons conduct heat well and plastic does not. High thermal conductivity is desirable for heat exchangers and thermal management while low thermal conductivity is needed for thermal insulation. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Nuclear electric propulsion (NEP) offers the potential to fundamentally expand the capability and reach of spacecraft, but realizing that potential requires overcoming significant challenges in reactor technology, power conversion and distribution, thermal management, electric propulsion, and system integration. These patterns encode the secrets of biological materials, such that similar patterns often emerge in different materials with similar functions. For example, a family of elastin proteins form stretchable fibers, which allow the constant movement of human skin, blood vessels, and lungs. We aim to decode the secrets of biological materials by investigating sequence patterns in repetitive proteins, towards establishing systematic protein sequence–biomaterial property relationships. This talk explores two classes of repetitive proteins as stimuli-responsive biopolymers. First, we investigate bacterial proteins that undergo conformational changes in response to calcium ions. We modify hydrophobicity, electrostatics, and sequence heterogeneity to demonstrate sequence-dependent, reversible folding and domain size changes in response to calcium ions. We also identify structural features that give rise to ion selectivity, which is not yet well-predicted by AI/ML tools. Second, we introduce enzymatic stimuli to drive isothermal phase separation of elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs). ELPs have drawn interest as heat-responsive biopolymers, such that ELPs undergo reversible phase separation from water upon heating. However, temperature is not always a convenient trigger, especially in biological environments that maintain near-constant temperature, pH, and ionic composition. To expand ELP function, we program a mechanism for isothermal phase separation upon proteolytic cleavage of a di-block ELP. This mechanism presents a new opportunity to exploit biological triggers for ELP phase behavior and self-assembly processes. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: In robotics, we have spent a lot of time building really good maps from noisy sensor data. Who doesn’t like a nice, crisp, globally consistent map? Over the last 20 years, I have been exploring a paradigm to robot navigation that eschews such globally consistent maps in favour of graphs of local maps, which are cheaper to construct, store, and query. These topometric maps enable so-called teach-and-repeat (T&R) navigation. In this talk, I will give a progress update on some of the new things we are doing with T&R including using different primary sensors, teaching with one robot and repeating with another, repeating with multiple robots together, and enabling end-user applications such as Arctic patrol and lunar cargo transport. Bio: Timothy Barfoot (University of Toronto Institute for Aerospace Studies – UTIAS) works in the area of autonomy for mobile robots targeting a variety of applications. He develops methods (localization, mapping, planning, control) to allow robots to operate over long periods of time in large-scale, unstructured, three-dimensional environments, using rich onboard sensing (e.g., cameras, laser rangefinders, radar) and computation. Timothy holds a BASc (9T6+PEY, Aerospace Option) from the UofT Engineering Science program and a PhD from UTIAS in robotics. He took up his academic position at UTIAS in May 2007, after spending four years at MDA Space (builder of the well-known Canadarm space manipulators), where he developed autonomous vehicle navigation technologies for both planetary rovers and terrestrial applications such as underground mining. He is a Fellow of the IEEE, a Fellow of the Canadian Academy of Engineering, held a Canada Research Chair for the full 10 years, was an Early Researcher Awardee in the Province of Ontario, and has received three paper awards at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2010, 2021, 2025) as well as four at the Conference on Robots and Vision (CRV 2014, 2016, 2023, 2025). Timothy began serving as Director (Dept. Head) of UTIAS on 1 July 2026, and previously served as Director of the UofT Robotics Institute,Director of the UofT Collaborative Specialization in Robotics, co-Faculty Advisor of UofT's self-driving car team that won the SAE Autodrivecompetition several times, Chair of the UofT Engineering Science Robotics Major, and was a Faculty Affiliate of the Vector Institute. He wasa Visiting Professor at the University of Oxford (2013, 2024) and worked as Director of Autonomous Systems at Apple in California (2017-9).He holds the position of Distinguished Engineer at Oxa Autonomy Ltd (parttime). He is the Editor in Chief of the IEEE Transactions on Field Robotics (T-FR), deputy EiC of the International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR), served on the Foundation Board of Robotics: Scienceand Systems (RSS), and served as the General Chair of Field and Service Robotics (FSR) 2015, which was held in Toronto. He is the author of State Estimation for Robotics (Cambridge 2017, 2024), which is free to download from his webpage, and co-editor/co-author of the SLAM Handbook (Cambridge 2026). All 5 of them came from new technologies, and two required space observatories. I’ll review the breakthrough ideas that grew into discoveries, and suggest where future technologies might go.The JWST is working brilliantly, and has found Little Red Dots, the current mystery object. But there’s still no Earth 2.0. The DKIST solar telescope with adaptive optics is working beautifully. The Vera Rubin Telescope is online, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will be launched just before this colloquium to study dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, and the 39 m diameter Extremely Large Telescope will be doing science around 2030. Among the new possibilities: the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a workhorse UV-near IR observatory with a coronagraph for exoplanets, and X-ray and far IR observatories from Probe class ($1B) to flagships. New detector and mirror technologies are making both exciting. The NAUTILUS concept will use molded glass lenses up to 8 m in diameter in space to collect light for spectroscopy. We’re also developing hybrid observatories combining telescopes and interferometers on the ground with satellites. The Landolt absolute photometric calibrator beacon will fly in 2029, and the CELESTE mission is a proposed Small Explorer to offer a laser beacon for adaptive optics to the ELT, giving it diffraction-limited image quality at visible wavelengths where the sky is darkest. An orbiting starshade could cast a star shadow on the ELT and enable imaging of another Earth in one minute. The Black Hole Explorer would extend the Event Horizon Telescope with an orbiting antenna could measure the spin of a black hole. If you can imagine it, you can build it.
